figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Classification of LLM benchmarks: We categorize along two dimensions: whether the questions are from a static dataset or a live, fresh source, and whether the evaluation metric relies on ground truth or (approximated) human preferences. MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), GSM-8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023b), and AlpacaEval (Li et al., 2023) are common examples of static benchmarks. Chatbot Arena is the platform introduced in this paper.
figures.headline: Benchmarks are classified by static or live questions and by ground-truth or human-preference metrics, with Chatbot Arena as the live, human-preference case.

We briefly review the common LLM benchmarks, following the classification presented in Figure 1.

figures.headline: Win rates and battle counts for a model subset show how pairwise votes are distributed across model pairs.

One critical goal is to estimate the win matrix: $\theta^{*}(a)=\mathbb{E}[H_{t}\mid A_{t}=a]$, for all $a\in\mathcal{A}$; see the left panel of Figure 2 for an illustration of the (empirical) win matrix.

citing_sentences: We present the top-16 topic clusters in Figure 3.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Intervals for the BT coefficients with and without multiplicity correction. The multiplicity correction, in this case a chi-square CLT interval, is technically required for the purpose of calculating the ranking, because it ensures all scores are simultaneously contained in their intervals (and the ranking is a function of all the scores). However, it induces extra conservatism, so we report both intervals.
figures.headline: Bradley-Terry coefficient intervals are shown with and without multiplicity correction, which adds conservatism.
citing_sentences: For this experiment, we ran a replay of $T=213,576$ historical votes from our online platform and calculate the BT coefficients using our earlier-described estimation algorithm with confidence intervals; see Figure 5 for these intervals (with and without multiplicity correction; the formal notion of approximate ranking technically requires multiplicity correction, but it makes the intervals looser).

figures.caption: Intervals for the BT coefficients as a function of the number of samples and the number of models $M$.
figures.headline: Uncorrected coefficient intervals keep coverage near the nominal level regardless of model count, while widths grow.
citing_sentences: A vector of BT coefficients is drawn, with each coordinate sampled i.i.d. from a distribution $\mathsf{beta}(1/\gamma,1/\gamma)$; we take $\gamma=2$ in Figure 6 (and we vary $\gamma$ in Appendix A).
The results can be seen in Figure 6 for the uncorrected intervals The coverage of the intervals behaves as expected, centering around $1-\alpha$, regardless of the number of models.

figures.caption: Interval widths on the win matrix (upper figure) and on the BT coefficients (lower figure) as a function of the number of samples, for random sampling and also adaptive sampling. Improvements from adaptive sampling can be seen in both cases, although they are more subtle on the scale of the score.
figures.headline: Adaptive sampling gives narrower intervals than random sampling for the win matrix, with a subtler gap for scores.
citing_sentences: The results are displayed in Figure 7.
One can see from the plots in Figure 7 that these results are not cherry-picked: the sample-efficiency of our method is better at all values on the horizontal axis.

The sandwich intervals, though larger in small samples, are more stable, and in large samples, they actually become smaller. (Coverage here is calculated with respect to the BT coefficient solution on the full dataset, so it is not as meaningful as in the simulation plot below.)

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have unlocked new capabilities and applications; however, evaluating the alignment with human preferences still poses significant challenges. To address this issue, we introduce Chatbot Arena, an open platform for evaluating LLMs based on human preferences. Our methodology employs a pairwise comparison approach and leverages input from a diverse user base through crowdsourcing. The platform has been operational for several months, amassing over 240K votes. This paper describes the platform, analyzes the data we have collected so far, and explains the tried-and-true statistical methods we are using for efficient and accurate evaluation and ranking of models. We confirm that the crowdsourced questions are sufficiently diverse and discriminating and that the crowdsourced human votes are in good agreement with those of expert raters. These analyses collectively establish a robust foundation for the credibility of Chatbot Arena. Because of its unique value and openness, Chatbot Arena has emerged as one of the most referenced LLM leaderboards, widely cited by leading LLM developers and companies. Our demo is publicly available at https://chat.lmsys.org.

sections.body: The introduction sorts LLM benchmarks by question source (static or live) and metric (ground truth or human preference). It argues that static, ground-truth benchmarks can become contaminated over time and that a definitive ground truth is sometimes unattainable for complex tasks. Chatbot Arena is a free website where a user asks any question, receives answers from two anonymous LLMs, and votes for the preferred response; model identities are shown only after voting. The authors report over 240K votes from about 90K users in over 100 languages as of Jan 2024. They also describe model-pair sampling algorithms meant to speed ranking convergence while retaining statistical validity.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Static benchmarks miss live human preferences, so Chatbot Arena collects pairwise votes from open crowdsourced use.

sections.body: This section reviews existing LLM benchmarks, including static multiple-choice and question-answering sets such as MMLU, HellaSwag and GSM-8K, and human-judged open-ended evaluations. It names contamination, saturation, overfitting and lack of human alignment as risks of static benchmarks, and cites DynaBench as a live, human-in-the-loop alternative for classical NLP tasks. Statistical ranking methods, including probability models and the Elo rating system used for LLMs, are summarized. Human preference datasets such as OpenAssistant and HH-RLHF are listed. The authors state that LMSYS-Chat-1M contains conversations but no human preference data, so it is unsuitable for direct use in ranking studies.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks are mostly static and ground-truth based, while live human-interaction evaluation was limited to specific organizations.

sections.body: The section describes the voting interface: users enter any prompt, see two anonymous model answers side by side, and vote for the better one, or choose tie or both are bad. Users must accept terms of use that allow public release of the data. Pairwise voting is used because a consistent absolute grading rubric is hard to set across many users. Collection began in April 2023 and covers more than 50 models, with 77% of conversations in English and 5% in Chinese. Model names and companies are removed by keyword filtering, and the OpenAI moderation API flags unsafe content, affecting 3% of requests. Non-uniform sampling concentrates votes on pairs with similar performance. Table 1 compares these statistics with other human preference datasets.
sections.heading: Human Preference Data Collection
sections.headline: Users compare two anonymous model answers to any prompt and vote, yielding around 240K votes from over 90K users.

sections.body: Ranking is framed as recovering model scores from pairwise outcomes. At each step the system serves a pair of models and observes a human response, and the win matrix gives the probability that one model is preferred over another for each pair. Models are scored by Bradley-Terry coefficients, estimated by minimizing binary cross-entropy; the authors chose these over Elo scores because they are better suited to statistical estimation. Tied models share the same rank. Under misspecification, maximum likelihood estimates remain asymptotically normal if the sandwich covariance is used. Appendix B adds a nonparametric extension that recovers the same coefficients when the logistic model is correct and remains valid for non-binary outcomes and non-transitive win rates.
sections.heading: From Pairwise Comparisons to Rankings
sections.headline: Ranking is defined from pairwise win probabilities using Bradley-Terry coefficients, which the authors prefer to Elo for statistical estimation.

sections.body: The win matrix is estimated by an inverse-probability-weighted mean, which the authors state is unbiased, with a covariance estimate and a central limit result under regularity conditions. Bradley-Terry coefficients come from reweighted maximum likelihood. Two interval methods are compared, the pivot bootstrap and sandwich standard errors; the authors deploy the sandwich intervals based on a simulation in Appendix A. For approximate rankings, a chi-squared confidence set is used so that, with probability at least 1 minus alpha, no model's performance is understated. Pairs are sampled in proportion to the reduction in confidence interval size. For anomalous users, per-vote p-values are combined with Fisher's test at randomly chosen points, which the authors describe as a heuristic that worked in small-scale tests.
sections.heading: Efficient Approximate Ranking
sections.headline: Adaptive pair sampling is specified with sandwich confidence intervals, and anomalous users are flagged by a Fisher-combined p-value test.

sections.body: Prompts are embedded with text-embedding-3-small and reduced from 1,536 to 5 dimensions using UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection). Hierarchical density-based clustering with minimum cluster size 32 then yields 600 clusters; the largest holds 1% of prompts and the rest fall below 0.5%. For 30 prompts from seven clusters, GPT-4 wins up to 97% against Llama-2-70b-chat in coding and reasoning clusters and below 60% in less demanding ones, judged by an LLM. For vote quality, experts relabeled 160 battles, taking 3-5 minutes each. Crowd-expert agreement is 72% to 83%, while expert-expert agreement is 79.4% and 89.8%. The authors attribute the 5%-10% gap mostly to crowd users overlooking factual errors.
sections.heading: Data Analysis
sections.headline: Crowd prompts span a long tail of topics, separate model strengths, and agree with expert votes at 72% to 83%.

sections.body: Ranking is tested on a replay of T=213,576 historical votes, with confidence intervals for the coefficients. Coverage is checked by simulation: coefficients are drawn from a beta distribution with gamma 2 over 20 trials, and uncorrected intervals center near the nominal level regardless of the number of models, while widths grow as models are added. For active sampling, the random baseline needs 54% and 5% more data than adaptive sampling to reach precision 0.2 for the win matrix and 0.3 for the score, respectively. The authors note the score-scale gain is more subtle. Anomalous-user detection used 25 manually identified anomalous users and 25 sampled normal users, reaching 90% true positive and 60-70% true negative rates. False negatives come from users who do not always behave abnormally.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Adaptive sampling needs 4,400 samples against 6,800 for random to reach win-matrix precision 0.2.

sections.body: The authors list limitations. The user base is expected to consist mainly of LLM hobbyists and researchers, which may bias the distribution of users. Prompts come from the online chat interface and may not match production or specialized-domain usage. The study measures helpfulness but not safety, which the authors say needs a parallel evaluation mechanism. Future work includes topic leaderboards, a section for multimodal and agent-based LLMs in gamified settings, and a more formal method for detecting harmful users based on nonnegative supermartingales and E-values. The E-value variants they tried did not perform well in power, so the current heuristic remains.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The authors note the user base may be biased toward hobbyists and researchers, data comes from one chat interface, and safety is not assessed.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the platform as an open system for evaluating LLMs through crowdsourced pairwise human preferences. The authors summarize their analysis of crowdsourced prompts and votes for diversity and quality, and their model sampling and ranking algorithm. They state that a dataset including 100K pairwise preference votes will be released for future research. The section presents no new experiments; the supporting evidence appears in the earlier sections.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Chatbot Arena is an open pairwise-vote platform, with a dataset of 100K votes planned for release.

sections.body: Appendix A compares bootstrap and sandwich confidence intervals on the 213576 replay data points and in simulations with gamma 2 and other gamma values. Appendix B defines a nonparametric Bradley-Terry score as an average over chains of pairings, which equals the Bradley-Terry coefficient when the logistic model is correct. Appendix C proves that the anomaly p-value is valid under exchangeability. Appendix D gives example prompts by cluster and the Arena Bench prompt set, with its judging procedure: 700 pairwise comparisons against GPT-3.5-Turbo-0301 across 350 user prompts, with two judgments per prompt to avoid positional bias. Examples of battles without ground truth close the appendix.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers a simulation comparing bootstrap and sandwich intervals, a nonparametric Bradley-Terry extension, a p-value proof, sample prompts, and the Arena Bench procedure.
